name: Esther Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the week, because I'm a shopfitter. I'm lead joiner for a fit-out firm, so we build the insides of shops, cafés and restaurants: counters, shelving, wall panels, the lot. A lot of it is nights, because the shopping centre won't let us work while customers are in, so I'll start at eight in the evening and finish at five. I like the detail, getting a walnut counter to meet a glass screen with no gap. I don't like eating dinner out of a van at two in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home and with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio flat I rent, near my mum, who I help out on weekends. I've got about three months of bills saved, which feels okay but not great when you're the only wage. Work's been thinner this year, honestly. Two of the big clothing chains we did fit-outs for have closed stores instead of refitting them. I don't use any AI stuff. I've got a phone for calls and the drawings, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd say now: there's no point getting worked up about every new thing they announce on the news. Some of it's real, most of it isn't. I'm not someone who posts online anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, AI fizzling doesn't fix my problem, because my problem is shops closing. Fewer fit-outs means fewer night shifts, and night shifts are where my extra money comes from. I've already gone from five nights a week to about three and a half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working every night they give me and stop saying no to the awkward jobs out of town. Cut back a bit, maybe cancel the gym and eat in more, to keep the three months from shrinking. And ask around about restaurant fit-out firms, because food places seem to be opening even when clothes shops close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Nothing to do with AI, just the work drying up slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've gone down to three and a half nights. What does that cost you each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 400 a month, give or take. I haven't touched savings yet, but I've stopped adding to them. Nobody needs a robot to take my job when the clothes shops are already closing faster than I can fit them out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you moved to a restaurant fit-out firm, what would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crew, mostly. Four people I trust, who I've trained myself. I'd hate to leave them, but I can't pay my rent with loyalty.

say: I'd say there's **no point** getting worked up over every news announcement.
I'd keep my views **offline**, as I always do.
think: My real problem is **shops closing**, not AI.
My night shifts have already dropped to about **three and a half** a week.
do: Take every **night shift**, including out-of-town jobs I used to refuse.
Cancel the **gym** and eat in more to protect savings.
Ask around **restaurant fit-out** firms for steadier work.
S0.quote: Nobody needs a robot to take my job when the clothes shops are already closing faster than I can fit them out.
fieldNote: She already carries a **400-a-month** drop in pay, before any AI change.
As the **only earner**, three months saved feels thin to her.
She weighs leaving a **loyal crew** against paying rent.

steps.text: Take every night shift offered, including out-of-town jobs
Cancel the gym and cook at home more
Ask restaurant fit-out firms about lead joiner work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is what it is. Shops will change, offices will change, and people like me will build whatever they need next. I'm not going to march about it, but I'm not going to cheer either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means even fewer shops. If AI handles the ordering and the customer questions online, the big chains close more stores, and every closed store is a fit-out I don't do. My hands are safe for a while, but my hours aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start applying to kitchen and bathroom firms that work on people's homes, because houses don't close. Save whatever I can, maybe 200 a month, by giving up the car and taking the night bus. I wouldn't learn any software unless a new boss made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but I'd be checking the work rota every Sunday with a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd give up the car. How would you get to night jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night buses, taxis on the bad nights, and lifts from Ricky on my crew. Selling my van to save money for a job that keeps disappearing feels like burning the furniture to heat the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if hours dropped further?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, honestly, even though I'm meant to be helping her. And my brother Pablo, who's a mechanic and always has cash. I'd hate asking, but I'd ask before I went into debt.

say: I'd say it is what it is and that **builders adapt** to new needs.
I'd neither **march** against it nor cheer it.
think: Online selling means **more closed stores**, so fewer fit-outs for me.
My hands are safe for a while, but my **hours** aren't.
do: Apply to **kitchen and bathroom** firms that work in people's homes.
Sell the **van** and use night buses to save 200 a month.
Avoid new **software** unless a new boss requires it.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot in her stomach every Sunday.
S1.quote: Selling my van to save money for a job that keeps disappearing feels like burning the furniture to heat the house.
fieldNote: Her hours could **realistically shrink**, and she's the only earner.
She sees the AI threat **indirectly**, through retail closures.
She'd lean on **family** before debt, but hates the idea.

steps.text: Apply to home kitchen and bathroom fitting firms
Sell the van and take night buses to save 200 a month
Ask her mum and brother Pablo for help if hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, not the government, not the bosses, not us. I don't trust either side to fix it, so I'd keep my head down and my mouth shut at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years the shops are run by AI and need fewer staff, and fewer staff means fewer shops worth fitting. Then robots by 2031 for the building itself. I'd be thirty-two and I'd probably be out of joinery, with nothing else on paper but a trade certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get out of shopfitting in the first year, into home kitchens or repair work for older people, which I think lasts longest. Save every spare penny, maybe 300 a month, even if it means moving back into my mum's spare room. And I'd stop thinking about buying anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like the floor's tilting and I can't find anything to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back to your mum's. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like going backwards ten years. At twenty-seven I'm the best joiner my firm has, and in the fast picture I'd be back in my mum's spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd avoid new technology. Would two years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If learning some program meant keeping a job, I'd learn it, gritting my teeth. But I don't believe one course would save me, so I'd rather put the effort into a different kind of work.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready**, not government, bosses or workers.
I'd keep my **head down** at work and not take sides.
think: Fewer shop staff means **fewer fit-outs** within two years.
I'd likely be **out of joinery** at thirty-two, with only a trade certificate.
do: Leave **shopfitting** in year one for home kitchens or repair work.
Save about **300 a month**, even by moving back to Mum's.
Drop any plan to **buy a home**.
S2.quote: At twenty-seven I'm the best joiner my firm has, and in the fast picture I'd be back in my mum's spare room.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her trade** and has only one income.
Moving back home feels like **going backwards** to her.
She doesn't trust **either side** of politics to help.

steps.text: Leave shopfitting for home kitchen or repair work in year one
Save about 300 a month from every spare shift
Move back into her mum's spare room
Lean on her brother Pablo for short-term cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not lose our heads. Somebody sensible will have to sort out rules, and I'd vote for whoever sounds sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the AI, eight for robots, so I'd be about thirty-five. Shops would be shrinking the whole time, though, so I'd feel it in my hours long before the robots arrive. It gives me time to move into home work properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move to a home kitchen fitting firm in the next eighteen months, while I'm still the senior person with a good name. Keep the van, because home jobs need one. Save 250 a month and try to get the cushion up to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had my hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move in eighteen months rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when the shop work really falls off, every shopfitter in town will be knocking on the same doors. I'd rather walk into a kitchen firm as the best joiner in town than crawl in as the fortieth shopfitter that month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about shopfitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big reveals. A café opening on a Saturday morning with my counter in it. Kitchens are nice too, but it's one family, not a queue out the door.

say: I'd tell people not to **lose their heads** with five years' warning.
I'd vote for whoever sounds most **sensible** on rules.
think: Shrinking shops would cut my **hours** long before robots arrive.
Five years gives me time to move into **home work** properly.
do: Move to a **home kitchen** firm within eighteen months.
Keep the **van**, since home jobs need one.
Save **250 a month** toward six months of cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, but with her hand on the wheel.
S3.quote: I'd rather walk into a kitchen firm as the best joiner in town than crawl in as the fortieth shopfitter that month.
fieldNote: She plans to move **early** to beat the rush, which is unusual for a resistant person.
Her hours still look likely to **shrink**, so anxious fits.
She'll miss the **public reveal** of a finished shop.

steps.text: Move to a home kitchen fitting firm within eighteen months
Save 250 a month toward a six-month cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so stop the scare stories. I'd tell younger joiners to learn home work as well as shop work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about forty when robots could do my job, and honestly the shops are the bigger threat in the meantime. With ten years, I could ease into kitchens without rushing. It'd still be on my mind, but it wouldn't run my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay in shopfitting a couple more years while the work's there, then move to kitchens. Save 150 a month steadily. Maybe help my mum sort her house so she can rent out a room, which helps us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there in the background, like a noise you stop hearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd actually move when the time came, or keep putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably put it off. I'm like that with change. Give me ten years of warning and I'll probably spend nine of them saying I'll sort it next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my boss lost another big contract. That's the real alarm clock for me, not anything about robots on the news.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so **stop the scare stories**.
I'd tell younger joiners to learn **home work** as well as shop work.
think: Robots reach my work at about **forty**; shops are the nearer threat.
I could ease into **kitchens** without rushing.
do: Stay in **shopfitting** two more years, then move to kitchens.
Help Mum **rent out a room** to help them both.
S4.quote: Give me ten years of warning and I'll probably spend nine of them saying I'll sort it next spring.
fieldNote: She admits she'd likely **put off** the move for years.
A **lost contract**, not news about robots, would make her act.
Her mood rests on **retail decline**, with AI a distant second.

steps.text: Keep shopfitting for two more years while work lasts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The shops would go and the robots would follow, and I'm on my own with three months saved. What would help is a firm that guarantees hours, or some kind of wage support between jobs that doesn't make you beg for it. When you're the only wage in the flat, three months of savings is not a cushion, it's a countdown with a calendar.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about nights. People forget that a lot of building work happens while everyone's asleep, and nobody's designing robots for that yet, as far as I know.

headlineQuote: When you're the only wage in the flat, three months of savings is not a cushion, it's a countdown with a calendar.
portrait: **Esther** is a 27-year-old **lead shopfitter** who fits out shops and cafés, mostly on night shifts.
She lives **alone** in a rented studio with about **three months** saved, near her mum.
Shop closures have already cut her **night shifts**, so she's uneasy even when nothing changes.
She **avoids AI** tools and sees the threat through retail decline more than robots.
Her plan in most pictures is to move into **home kitchen** fitting, though she admits she'd delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because shops and then robots would hit her single income **fast**.
whatWouldHelp: **Guaranteed hours** or wage support between jobs, without begging for it.
